Insurance Pitfalls of the Pandemic

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Many business owners believed their business interruption insurance would pay out due to the Covid-19 pandemic, only to find insurers reluctant to dock up after lockdown.

Unique Selling Point:
We have had many web submissions from business owners, particularly in the tourism and hospitality industry, who thought they were covered for exactly the kind of crisis the national lockdown and Corona Virus Pandemic has caused by their business interruption insurance. Most of them were sold on lines from brokers such as "if your business closes for a month, your fully covered" etc. But now that they've been forced to close their lodges, restaurants and B&B's and claimed from insurers like Momentum, Santam and Brite, the insurers have come up with any number of excuses not to pay.

Summary:
This is not a uniquely South African problem, insurers all over the world are scrambling to cover claims - with some in the US claiming the insurance industry can't afford to pay. Locally it seems this is also the case - and businesses like restaurants and hotels, who are going to be the hardest hit in the economic fall out of the lockdown and virus, are getting the short end of the stick. We'll deal with the merits of each case study on a case by case basis, because it all boils down to the fine print. BUT - no matter what the fine print says, all these owners have been docking up thousands of rands in premiums for years, all in the belief that they WERE covered. Even once lockdown is eventually lifted, these businesses, which form an integral part of the economy, are going to be vulnerable. The insurance could have at least covered some of their costs - costs that will impact on thousands of lives as staff, many of them breadwinners, face layoffs and cut salaries.

Further information:
We have received complaints mainly against Momentum/Santam and Brite insurance.

Morag Maynard is the owner of the Zoolakes Sports Club and Pannetone Cafe in Parkwood JHB. They submitted a claim of "consequential loss" for the full loss of income because of the lockdown to Bryte insurance. Their policy documentation states: "that there is a three month insurance cover for loss of income due to (d): "notifiable disease within 50km of the premises stated in the schedule". But Bryte are refusing to pay out, claiming interpretation of the policy does not cover Corona Virus

Ashley Bloxham is the owner of the St Ives lodge and venue in the KZN Midlands, who has claimed from Santam for the same thing. He was covered for R8.8 million which included dread disease - his broker believes his claim should have been paid out. But Santam have said that someone with Covid-19 would have had to stayed at the lodge, and the lodge closed because of that, for them to pay. Not a lockdown caused by the Corona Virus.

Erika Rautenbach is the owner of the Surval Boutique guesthouse in Oudstshoorn with the same problem. She has claimed from Santam, who have refused to pay unless they can prove someone within a 50km radius of the guesthouse has had Corona Virus and forced them to close. Not lockdown.

There are many more of the same.

NB VERY INTERESTINGLY, BOTH BRITE AND SANTAM HAVE ADVISED POLICY HOLDERS THAT ANY DREAD DISEASE COVER IN THEIR POLICIES WILL FALL AWAY FROM 1 JUNE 2020. IN A WAY THEY ARE ADMITTING THAT THEY CANNOT COVER EVENTS OF THIS MAGNITUDE, WHILE FOR THE PAST DECADES THEY'VE BEEN TAKING PEOPLE'S MONEY FOR IT.

PRODUCTION NOTES:
I AM PLANNING ON GIVING CASE STUDIES IN OTHER PROVINCES A VIDEO TUTORIAL ON HOW TO FILM MANY OF THE VISUALS WE WILL NEED FOR US ON THEIR CELLPHONES. I ALSO WANT TO FILM THE SKYPE/ZOOM INTERVIEWS WITH THEM RECORDING ON THEIR PHONES FOR BETTER QUALITY. JHB CASE STUDIES AND HOPEFULLY CONFRONTS CAN BE FILMED IN PERSON WITH PROTOCOLS OBSERVED.

Script:


Covid and Business Interruption Insurance
First Draft Script
23 May 2020

Voice
The tourism and hospitality industries have been amongst the hardest hit by the global Covid-19 pandemic. Once thriving businesses now stand empty. And while a large part of our economy reopens on monday, that won’t be the case for many restaurants, hotels and guesthouses.

Link Derek
Business interruption insurance policies cover companies for loss of income if they are forced to close due to unforeseen events. As the pandemic hit our shores, many business owners turned to their insurance providers for help. But weeks into the national lockdown, they’re still waiting for answers

Voice
Morag Maynard owns the Zoo Lakes Sport Club in Johannesburg. Pre-lockdown, they hosted hundreds of sporting enthusiasts and their families every week.

Sound Up Morag
Derek: Morag it must be an eery feeling coming back here, what’s it like normally?

Morag: Normally full of activity. Kids running through, we’ve got a play area there. We’ve got generally sport 7 days a week on our field. This is heart breaking, it’s like the life and the soul of the club have been sucked out.

Voice
Just under an hour’s drive away in Pretoria, the breakfast room at the Hatfield Guest House is deserted. Owner Scott Cochrane says the lockdown couldn’t have come at a worse time.

Sound Up Scott
Derek: Scott it must be upsetting for you to walk around here and it’s just desolate?

Scott: Absolutely, I mean we were expecting to have some of our busiest months coming up to June. A total change of landscape you know.

Voice
Maynard says she’s lost hundreds of thousands due to the national lockdown.

Sound Up Morag
Morag: You know this is a big premises, we have capacity for 600 or 700 people for sport, our overheads are big.

Derek: But you have an insurance policy?

Morag: We do, we do. And we thought we could count on that. You know you take insurance for emergencies and ja, it hasn’t turned out that way.

Link Derek
Unfortunately, standard business interruption insurance won’t cover most companies for losses incurred from infectious disease outbreaks - Unless they have specific extensions covering it in their policies.


Voice
Andre’ Coetzee from Urban Insurance Brokers has more than two decades experience in the industry - he says most business interruption policies only cover physical damage to premises.

Sound Up Andre’
General business interruption is activated when there is a defined event, or a material loss such as a fire, explosion or storm damage.

Voice
But some policies contain extensions, clauses which provide extra cover to specified losses outside of the general coverage offered.

Sound Up Andre’
Some insurers may charge a premium for it, some insurers may give it to you free of charge.

Voice
Maynard says her policy, from Bryte Insurance, does have an extension covering disease, and it reads:

Sound Up Morag
“A notifiable disease, occurring within a radius of 50 kilometers of the premises stated in the schedule.” That is the only criterion in the whole policy.

Voice
Covid-19 has been declared a notifiable disease, and there are currently hundreds of confirmed cases within a 50km radius of the sports club. But weeks after lodging her claim, Morag says the outcome is still pending, because her insurers keep asking for new information.

Sound Up Morag
And every time we submit one form we get sent another form.

Voice
In this email from her brokers the loss adjuster requires: - the date or dates of the specific outbreak/s, -the situation addresses of the specific outbreak/s and -details of the affected persons.

Sound Up Morag
Derek: So they’re virtually asking for details of people who’ve been infected in this area?

Morag: Absolutely yes.

Derek: As if, aren’t the figures out there every day?

Morag: Well I would think so and its published in terms of stats not names, I can’t see what knowing a specific name is going to make a difference.

Voice
Scott Cochrane says while he desperately needs the money now, his claim is also still pending with his insurers Factory and Industrial. His policy schedule also lists a business interruption extension which says: “notifiable disease occurring within a radius of 50km of the premises”.

Sound Up Scott
Scott: They were saying that for our cover to kick in, the viral threat would have to originate from our business. Start at our business, so much so that they were saying I should have tested our staff and guests for Covid-19.

Derek: But would you have had any medical tests done?

Scott: I wouldn’t of financially been able to you know, test everybody that comes into my premises. They would never agree to that in any case.

Voice
Cochrane has now taken his case to the Ombudsman for Short Term Insurance. The St Ives Lodge in the KZN Midlands is a popular tourist destination, wedding venue and restaurant. Owner Ashley Bloxham says his policy from Santam had the same kind of extension, but his insurer also hasn’t resolved his claim because of similar requests for information.

Sound Up Ashley
Ashley: Over the phone Derek I’ve been told that I would have had to have had a Covid-19 positive on the property and we would have to have had then closed down so that we could sanitise the place and they would only cover me for the time that we were closed for sanitary purposes.

Link Derek
But in cases where specific extensions covering disease outbreaks do exist, and claimants are in obvious financial distress, why are claims not being expedited? Regrettably none of the insurers from our three case studies were willing to come on camera to answer that.

Voice
They did however respond in writing. In general insurers are interpreting the extensions to only be valid if a business suffered losses due to a specific case of Covid-19 at their premises, and not because they’ve been forced to close by government’s national lockdown. It’s a stance that’s been noted by the two South African Insurance industry regulators, the Financial Sector Conduct Authority and the Reserve Bank’s Prudential Authority. Viviene Pearson is the CEO of the South African Insurance Association. She says insurers will pay out on valid claims where all the conditions have been met.

Sound Up Viviene
And I do want to emphasise that those straightforward claims, with all the conditions being met etc, will be paid.

Voice
But how the conditions are interpreted may eventually have to be settled in a court of law. Dewald Cillie is the managing director of SATIB Insurance Brokers, who specialise in offering insurance to the tourism industry.

Sound Up Dewald
Derek: Why wouldn’t you have a claim Dewald, if you’ve got a specific clause stating infectious or notifiable diseases?

Dewald: Its a very contentious question at this stage. And there is many legal opinion around the wording of these extensions. The view of the insurers at this stage is that it never was the intention to have a policy respond to this world and global pandemic that we currently have.

Derek: But Dewald, surely it was up to the insurers to put in their own clause that this doesn’t apply to a lockdown, to a pandemic?

Dewald: Absolutely, and I suppose this is where this matter will become a legal matter in the end of the day. And I’ve got no doubt that this will be challenged in court to various degrees and levels.

Sound Up Andre’
I really think the insurers out there are going to have a hard time proving their case in a court of law as their wording are generally worded very poorly, it’s non specific and open to interpretation.

Voice
In Scott Cochrane’s case, his insurers Factory and Industrial said they’d sought legal counsel on the claim and believed their handling of the claim was correct.

Link Derek
They also said that if Scott wanted to take the matter further “there are numerous alternative complaint processes available, which alternative processes include referral to the Ombudsman for Short-term Insurance, the FSCA, our internal complaint procedures, the South African Insurance Association, or even going as far as instituting legal action.”

Sound Up Scott
Most business people wouldn’t be in a position to go the route that they are suggesting with litigation.

Voice
Maynard says she’s been told that in future her insurers will no longer cover infectious diseases.

Sound Up Morag
From the 1st of June our premiums and our policy is due for the annual renewal. They sent out documentation stating that from the first of June that no Corona Virus, or Sars, Avian Flu, any related mutations, shall be covered.

Voice
Ashley Bloxham says they’ve had a similar letter from Santam.

Link Derek
But policy holders say they feel that’s tantamount to the insurers admitting that they were covered previously.

Sound Up Morag
But what I want to know is, if it’s not covered from the 1st of June, surely by default it was covered pre 1st of June?

Voice
Cillie says South African insurers have been put under pressure to make the changes to policies by their re-insurers - the companies who in turn insure them against major claim events.

Sound Up Dewald
We are aware, or it has come to our knowledge, that the re-insurance backing that insurers had in the past, have now retracted their support in terms of Covid-19.

Voice
Maynard’s insurers, Bryte Insurance said: “To date, we have paid more than 750 valid claims amounting to R22 million to our clients in the hospitality sector, the majority of which related to the cancellation of bookings for accommodation.” They also said that they were waiting to receive further information they’d requested from her before they could continue with their assessment of her claim.


Sound Up Morag
And then blow me down yesterday we get another template, it’s altered from the first template, and its just the ballpark is changing the whole time.

Link Derek
Ashley Bloxham’s insurers, Santam said:
“As with the majority of our counterparts in the short-term insurance industry locally and globally, our Contingent Business Interruption and Cancellation of Bookings policies do not cover pandemics. The reality is that no insurer can afford to offer widespread pandemic coverage within its standard policies, the premiums would be too high and it would become unaffordable for the majority of businesses.”

Sound Up Viviene
You cannot increase the premium to cover a potential huge risk, or huge loss, by making the premium unaffordable. So that’s the reason why these kinds of conditions and so on do exist.

Voice
For now the sad reality for business owners like Maynard, who’ll remain closed for the foreseeable future, is there simply doesn’t seem to be enough support out there.

Sound Up Morag
Derek: Do you think there’s a distinct danger you might have to give up the business?

Morag: Absolutely. Without a doubt.





Promo 1
Voice
Their small business is on the ropes and they can’t afford to pay their staff. Their salvation was specific business interruption insurance. But the next battle is getting paid out.

Promo 2
Voice
Unable to operate until the lockdown ends, many businesses in the tourism and hospitality industries thought they’d be covered by their insurers - only to be left in the lurch.

Promo 3
Voice
As a small business owner you’d hope your business interruption insurance would tide you over during lockdown. But how sure are you you’re covered for a global pandemic?

They sent out documentation stating that from the first of June that no Corona Virus, or Sars, Avian Flu, any related mutations, shall be covered. Voice Ashley Bloxham says they’ve had a similar letter from Santam. Link Derek But policy holders say they feel that’s tantamount to the insurers admitting that they were covered previously. Sound Up Morag But what I want to know is, if it’s not covered from the 1st of June, surely by default it was covered pre 1st of June? Voice Cillie says South African insurers have been put under pressure to make the changes to policies by their re-insurers - the companies who in turn insure them against major claim events. Sound Up Dewald We are aware, or it has come to our knowledge, that the re-insurance backing that insurers had in the past, have now retracted their support in terms of Covid-19. Voice Maynard’s insurers, Bryte Insurance said: “To date, we have paid more than 750 valid claims amounting to R22 million to our clients in the hospitality sector, the majority of which related to the cancellation of bookings for accommodation.” They also said that they were waiting to receive further information they’d requested from her before they could continue with their assessment of her claim. Sound Up Morag And then blow me down yesterday we get another template, it’s altered from the first template, and its just the ballpark is changing the whole time. Link Derek Ashley Bloxham’s insurers, Santam said: “As with the majority of our counterparts in the short-term insurance industry locally and globally, our Contingent Business Interruption and Cancellation of Bookings policies do not cover pandemics. The reality is that no insurer can afford to offer widespread pandemic coverage within its standard policies, the premiums would be too high and it would become unaffordable for the majority of businesses.” Sound Up Viviene You cannot increase the premium to cover a potential huge risk, or huge loss, by making the premium unaffordable. So that’s the reason why these kinds of conditions and so on do exist. Voice For now the sad reality for business owners like Maynard, who’ll remain closed for the foreseeable future, is there simply doesn’t seem to be enough support out there. Sound Up Morag Derek: Do you think there’s a distinct danger you might have to give up the business? Morag: Absolutely. Without a doubt. Promo 1 Voice Their small business is on the ropes and they can’t afford to pay their staff. Their salvation was specific business interruption insurance. But the next battle is getting paid out. Promo 2 Voice Unable to operate until the lockdown ends, many businesses in the tourism and hospitality industries thought they’d be covered by their insurers - only to be left in the lurch. Promo 3 Voice As a small business owner you’d hope your business interruption insurance would tide you over during lockdown. But how sure are you you’re covered for a global pandemic?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Many business owners believed their business interruption insurance would pay out due to the Covid-19 pandemic, only to find insurers reluctant to dock up after lockdown.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have had many web submissions from business owners, particularly in the tourism and hospitality industry, who thought they were covered for exactly the kind of crisis the national lockdown and Corona Virus Pandemic has caused by their business interruption insurance. Most of them were sold on lines from brokers such as "if your business closes for a month, your fully covered" etc. But now that they've been forced to close their lodges, restaurants and B&B's and claimed from insurers like Momentum, Santam and Brite, the insurers have come up with any number of excuses not to pay.
metadata.Summary: This is not a uniquely South African problem, insurers all over the world are scrambling to cover claims - with some in the US claiming the insurance industry can't afford to pay. Locally it seems this is also the case - and businesses like restaurants and hotels, who are going to be the hardest hit in the economic fall out of the lockdown and virus, are getting the short end of the stick. We'll deal with the merits of each case study on a case by case basis, because it all boils down to the fine print. BUT - no matter what the fine print says, all these owners have been docking up thousands of rands in premiums for years, all in the belief that they WERE covered. Even once lockdown is eventually lifted, these businesses, which form an integral part of the economy, are going to be vulnerable. The insurance could have at least covered some of their costs - costs that will impact on thousands of lives as staff, many of them breadwinners, face layoffs and cut salaries.
metadata.Further information: We have received complaints mainly against Momentum/Santam and Brite insurance. Morag Maynard is the owner of the Zoolakes Sports Club and Pannetone Cafe in Parkwood JHB. They submitted a claim of "consequential loss" for the full loss of income because of the lockdown to Bryte insurance. Their policy documentation states: "that there is a three month insurance cover for loss of income due to (d): "notifiable disease within 50km of the premises stated in the schedule". But Bryte are refusing to pay out, claiming interpretation of the policy does not cover Corona Virus Ashley Bloxham is the owner of the St Ives lodge and venue in the KZN Midlands, who has claimed from Santam for the same thing. He was covered for R8.8 million which included dread disease - his broker believes his claim should have been paid out. But Santam have said that someone with Covid-19 would have had to stayed at the lodge, and the lodge closed because of that, for them to pay. Not a lockdown caused by the Corona Virus. Erika Rautenbach is the owner of the Surval Boutique guesthouse in Oudstshoorn with the same problem. She has claimed from Santam, who have refused to pay unless they can prove someone within a 50km radius of the guesthouse has had Corona Virus and forced them to close. Not lockdown. There are many more of the same. NB VERY INTERESTINGLY, BOTH BRITE AND SANTAM HAVE ADVISED POLICY HOLDERS THAT ANY DREAD DISEASE COVER IN THEIR POLICIES WILL FALL AWAY FROM 1 JUNE 2020. IN A WAY THEY ARE ADMITTING THAT THEY CANNOT COVER EVENTS OF THIS MAGNITUDE, WHILE FOR THE PAST DECADES THEY'VE BEEN TAKING PEOPLE'S MONEY FOR IT.
